I'm not sure if it's because I've applied this on top of to 4.5.1 (doubt it), but I can't get this to work from inside the abstract class or child abstract classes which don't implement the method. It only seems to work from a different class on a new project. In an existing project I have I'm still getting the warning from other classes as well.

It makes sense that it does not suppress the warning in a child class that implements the method, but the abstract class and any child abstract classes that do not implement the method need to suppress the warning as well.

> It makes sense that it does not suppress the warning in an inherited class that implements the method, but the abstract class and any inherited abstract classes that do not implement the method need to suppress the warning as well.

Hi @Kaleb-Reid , please could you provide an example script that demonstrates this problem? I am struggling to replicate 😄

@wheatear-dev Is it because the test is being run on an abstract class? Not really familiar with tests but my guess is the test is trying to instantiate ClassB or ABC and call ```test()``` on it which you can't do.

Okay - it is no longer segfaulting, but it is replicating the bug, and hence the tests are failing.

Might have to step back from this, since I'm genuinely lost on how to proceed.

If anyone has guidance, please shout 😄

@wheatear-dev The problem is that ```get_function_signature()``` is not finding the method, making ```found``` false. I think that the third argument to it may be incorrect because it seems like it needs to be the ```DataType``` of the class which the method belongs to?

Looks like `p_await->datatype.to_string()` always return `null`, so `get_function_signature` cannot find correct `base_type`. When using `parser->current_class->get_datatype()` as `base_type`, I can ease one of four warnings.

(deleted out-of-date codes)

But I think the other three are not `abstract` method, Maybe they are not this PR's problem?

@xuhuisheng I was under the impression that ```parser->current_class``` in this context is class containing the await, therefore it will only find the function definition when the await is inside the abstract class. It needs to somehow derive the ```ClassNode``` for the abstract class from the ```AwaitNode``` if that's possible.

Also I think the other three warnings still should be fixed by this pr. I assume the warning that went away was the one on line 11 and the difference between that one and the remaining ones is that the function is defined in that class as abstract so ```parser->current_class``` is the correct class and ```get_function_definition()``` finds the function. The other warnings remain because the method is not defined directly in the class that has the warning but ```parser->current_class``` points to it anyways.

@xuhuisheng They are abstract though. ```ABCLocal```, ```ABC```, and ```ABCChild``` are the static types of the variables ```l```, ```a```, and ```b``` respectively, which are all abstract. I didn't test but if you changed the static types of the variables to the concrete type of the object which gets assigned to them I would guess that the warnings would go away because they are implemented as coroutines.

@Kaleb-Reid 

Yes, you are right. After changing their type declaration from `super class` to 'sub class', the warnings disappeared. Looks like GDScript used declared type not real class type to choose function declaration.
﻿
I will go on digging.

Thanks everyone, and especially @xuhuisheng for your code, that also passes for me locally.

I'm currently rebasing onto the `master` branch, and will push when I confirm that it's still passing.

P.S. - sorry for waiting over a week to reply, I've been super unwell 😓

Hi @nathancarter 👋 

Thanks for your reply. It's nice to see people's enthusiasm for our work! 😌

When I'm home, I'll rebase this PR branch, fix any problems, and then try to find a reviewer on the contributors chat.

Caveat though... it could still be a while longer. 😅
Is there any proposal on this change? I'm personally not convinced that it is a better solution than providing some way to mark abstract methods as co-routine.

> Is there any proposal on this change? 

Great question.

I found a couple of candidates, but neither are both exactly aligned and popular:

- godotengine/godot-proposals#5893
    - proposes an optional `@async` annotation
    - but when `@async` is not applied, the gdscript analyzer will still have no way to determine if an `@abstract` method is awaitable
- godotengine/godot-proposals#8363
    - proposes an `.is_async()` method on `Callable`
    - likely can't address this use case on its own, since it's a helper and doesn't provide additional information on whether an `@abstract` method is awaitable

> I'm personally not convinced that is a better solution than providing some way to mark abstract methods as co-routine.

There is a tradeoff here, no matter how we would mark methods - abstract or otherwise - as a coroutine.

Either this "marking" is mandatory, and gdscript analyzer will always have that info, making this PR redundant in purpose.

Or this "marking" is optional, and in its absence, this PR will remain needed to ensure gdscript analyzer does not raise this warning wrongly.
I don't really understand the two cases you describe. Suppose the logic for marking was `annotated_with("async") or body_has_await()`, what would be the issue here?

> I don't really understand the two cases you describe.

The problem this PR tries to solve is surfacing enough information to gdscript analyzer that such false positives are eliminated.

> Suppose the logic for marking was `annotated_with("async")`

This is closer, but is what I meant by optional. If this becomes the signal that an abstract method is a coroutine, then when/if it is absent, the error will still fire.

There would still not be enough information in that case.

Making such an annotation mandatory would be a breaking change to the syntax of gdscript, and that proposal doesn't seem very popular.


> or `body_has_await()`

This won't work for methods decorated with `@abstract`, since they don't need to declare a body.
The or was meant as in a boolean expression.

> The or was meant as in a boolean expression.

I addressed the second condition separately as it is never true in this case.

Abstract methods should not specify bodies.

I'll try to consolidate these replies as on, coming back to this, mine are a mess. I am sorry @HolonProduction, and will do better.

Before that, I'd like to thank the maintainers. You are all under so much pressure, and it's really good of you to read these little PRs.

Please let me try again:

> Is there any proposal on this change?

No. This PR was intended as a small bugfix, and has more tests than actual code.

> I'm personally not convinced that it is a better solution than providing some way to mark abstract methods as co-routine.

Having set this aside for a few weeks, I appreciate your point of view so much more.

I don't see any realistic and popular proposal for such a feature right now, but that does not imply:

1. This "bugfix" is appropriate, even as a stopgap
2. That the maintainers are required to accept it

> Suppose the logic for marking was `annotated_with("async") or body_has_await()`

My first reply to this was clumsy.

> The or was meant as in a boolean expression.

I still can't see how `body_has_await()` is anything other than `false` for an `@abstract` method, as these shouldn't declare bodies at all.

Given that - logically - `first_condition() or false` is equivalent to just `first_condition()`, I therefore ignored it. My reply did not explain that well.

### Closing comments

To eliminate the need for this error entirely, my read is that we would require both:

1. An `@async` annotation for coroutines
2. It to be mandatory, at least for `@abstract` coroutines

I will always answer your questions. Thanks for reading.
